name: The Clever Hans Effect
statement: An observer's own unconscious cues can lead a subject (human or animal) to produce responses the observer subtly expects.
statementAccent: unconscious cues can lead a subject
meaning: The Clever Hans effect names how a questioner’s involuntary body-language signals can guide a subject to give an apparently correct or expected answer, without the subject actually having the ability being tested. It is a foundational case of the observer-expectancy effect in experimental methodology.
mechanism: A trainer or questioner unintentionally tenses or relaxes posture, breathing, or facial expression as the subject approaches the correct answer; the subject learns to use these micro-cues as a stopping signal. Because neither party is aware of the cueing, the exchange looks like the subject possesses the tested competence when it actually reflects behavioural reading of the observer.

examples.text: Clever Hans, owned by Wilhelm von Osten, appeared to solve arithmetic and calendar problems by tapping his hoof, drawing public and press attention including New York Times coverage in 1904.

In his 1907 investigation, Oskar Pfungst found Hans answered correctly about 89% of the time when the horse could see the questioner, but only about 6% when the questioner was hidden — showing the answers depended on visual cues, not calculation.

Pfungst observed that questioners’ posture and expression grew subtly tense as Hans’s tapping approached the correct count, then relaxed at the right number — an involuntary signal Hans used to know when to stop.

whyItMatters: The case became a cautionary model in research design, showing how experimenter or trainer expectations can unintentionally bias results in animal cognition, psychology, and beyond — leading to practices like blind and double-blind testing.
limits: The effect describes unconscious cueing specifically; it does not mean all apparently intelligent animal behaviour is fraudulent, nor that the trainer was deceptive — Pfungst concluded the cueing was unintentional.
misreadings: It is sometimes misreported as a deliberate hoax by the trainer, when Pfungst’s investigation concluded von Osten was unaware he was signalling the horse.
origin: Named after the horse Clever Hans, exhibited in Germany by Wilhelm von Osten in the early 1900s; psychologist Oskar Pfungst investigated and explained the phenomenon in 1907.

sources.text: Clever Hans, Wikipedia. — von Osten’s ownership, the public exhibitions, and Pfungst’s 1907 visibility experiments with accuracy figures.
Oskar Pfungst, Wikipedia. — his identity and role in the 1907 investigation.
